title: Anti-Pattern: Read Replicas Without Sharding
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
I’d had this topic in mind to write about for a long time. On Tuesday, during an internal webinar on MongoDB replication hosted by our product management team, I got more insights and added some notes. By Thursday, the web was praising an architecture that implements this exact anti‑pattern. It's the occasion to finish and publish this: scaling with read replicas quickly hits its limits unless you consider sharding first.

Availability and Consistency

In the following diagram, a single primary server (the only one that can serve consistent reads and writes) sends its WAL to a cascade of read replicas. Having a single primary in a large database is problematic because failures or upgrades can cause extended downtime. While read replicas can still handle read requests during network partitions, the cascading replication hierarchy can lead to consistency issues across a large part of the cluster. This, in turn, may reduce availability when replication lag becomes unacceptable.

MongoDB addresses these problems through online upgrades and by retrieving logs from any secondary, but a different issue remains common in all databases when read replicas are added before sharding.

RAM usage

Without sharding or workload separation, load balancers direct queries to any read replica, increasing global connections and CPU usage, but not global memory efficiency. Balanced queries on the same dataset must load the frequently accessed data into memory on all instances. Scaling up increases in-memory data capacity, but scaling out without sharding doesn't. It keeps the same data, table, and indexes on all instances, offering no advantage in RAM utilization. With 50 read replicas, you incur 50 times the necessary memory costs without gaining performance benefits. The most important in a compute instance is shared memory, as accessing shared data is the primary purpose of a database.

With PostgreSQL, these frequently used blocks are doubled on each server: the PostgreSQL shared buffers and the Linux filesystem buffers. In a 50-read-replica cluster, there are 102 copies of the same block in memory. If you double the cluster size, you will use twice as much memory without any performance advantage, since each replica must contain the same data. MongoDB also uses both caching, but for different formats: fast access to mutable BSON in the WiredTiger memory, and a compressed, minimal version in the Linux cache, which holds more data. Still, you don't want the same data in memory across all servers.

Read workload separation

Most load balancers, like listing multiple hosts in a connection string, just do round-robin. They don’t route queries based on filters or server load. To really optimize read replicas, you need smarter routing and dedicated nodes aligned with your data and workload. For example, you can send recent-data queries to one pool and analytical queries on history to another. You can also extract a key—such as tenant ID—from query filters and route those queries to a subset of replicas. This is similar to sharding, but only for reads, and can improve memory usage.

Still, workload separation is not enough, as all replicas receive the same write operations from the primary and apply them to the shared memory buffers. With a single primary, all table and index writes are replicated to every read replica and pass through the same database cache and OS buffers. Even replicas dedicated to a specific data set, like a tenant or a past year, must use memory to apply the writes from other tenants and recent dates, even if they never receive queries for that data under your read-sharding scheme. It's good that a synchronous read replica used for high availability has a warm cache in case of failover, but you don't need 50 copies of that warm cache.

Why did they do that?

Many readers of the OpenAI blog article have been misled by the title without reading or understanding the full context:

What the article explains is that they truly moved the critical write-heavy workload to a sharded document database - CosmosDB - on Azure, given their partnership with Microsoft. If you look at real-world scaling solutions, they are all NoSQL solutions, even when implemented on SQL databases. OpenAI applied all of them, as mentioned in their article: sharding, eventual consistency, cascading read replicas, lazy writes, upfront caching, write throttling, limiting create and alter table, flexible JSON, avoiding joins with too many tables... Most of the "Scaling PostgreSQL" in this article involves moving away from PostgreSQL, or at least to a proprietary fork like CosmosDB.

So why did they deploy this massive single-primary cluster with 50 read replicas? As the article explains, sharding a SQL application is hard if it isn’t planned from the start:

sharding existing application workloads would be highly complex and time-consuming

Sharding is easy with a document model, and that's what they did on CosmosDB. However, for legacy applications that don't want to invest in the data model, they stayed on PostgreSQL with a single primary deployment, paying the price of memory amplification.

While serving 800 million users is impressive, the PostgreSQL scenario is limited to a read-mostly workload, with applications that require no changes. It’s also important to consider the financial context of their decision: OpenAI’s partnership with Microsoft and its familiarity with high memory consumption mean that the high cost of provisioning all instances with large memory on Azure may not be a significant concern for them.

While such an article is interesting to understand the problems, what has been a good decision for them doesn't apply to others. The risk with this title is thinking we can run a monolithic PostgreSQL instance with millions of users, which is incorrect. Look at AWS, which manages many critical PostgreSQL applications at scale. You'll find that Amazon Aurora limits the number of read replicas to 15, even though replication is more efficient than standard PostgreSQL, since only metadata is transmitted by the primary, with replicas reading from distributed storage. There are good reasons to design for sharding long before reaching this limit.

OpenAI's decisions for their existing applications shouldn't dictate your application's design. If you think you will need to scale with read replicas, plan for sharding now.

Sharding before read replicas

For the reasons exposed above, true scalability must involve sharding on the primary before adding read replicas. Instead of one primary with 50 read replicas, you may use 10 primaries with four read replicas each, and smaller instances. Not only does this provide better consistency and high availability, especially with a Raft-based database, as each shard is resilient to two failures, but it also allows smaller instances in terms of storage and memory. for any database.

Here are the advantages of sharding before using read replicas:

  • Availability: ❌ Single point of failure → ✅ Failures limited to 1/Nth
  • Consistency: ⚠️ Lag hits all replicas → ✅ Lag only within shard
  • Memory use: ❌ Same data everywhere → ✅ Only the shard’s data cached
  • Blast radius: ❌ 100% of users affected → ✅ 1/Nth affected
  • Write scale: ❌ All writes to one node → ✅ Writes split across shards

In my view, memory consumption is often the most overlooked aspect. Simply adding read replicas to a single primary doesn't improve memory scalability because each replica needs to maintain the same working set, both for load-balanced reads and for applying writes from the primary. This applies to all databases, SQL or NoSQL, and finding a sharding key is part of data modeling. If you are on MongoDB, the hierarchical nature of the document model makes sharding easier, and the drivers are shard-aware. If you are on PostgreSQL, sharding may involve some denormalization, and should also be planned upfront.
